title: Piping
body:
A pipe is a one-way byte channel between two processes: one writes to one end, the other
reads from the other end, and the bytes come out in the order they went in. It is the
shell-level form of [[Message Passing]], and the thing you have been using in the
[[Shell]] the whole time without calling it IPC:

```bash
ls -l | grep '\.md$' | wc -l
```

Three processes running **at the same time**, not one after the other. `ls` writes as it
goes, `grep` reads as it goes; the shell does not wait for `ls` to finish first.

## What the kernel is actually doing

The pipe is a fixed-size buffer in kernel memory, and the two ends are ordinary
[[File System Interface|file descriptors]], which is why a program can `read` and `write` a
pipe without knowing it is not a [[File]]. That buffer makes it a
[[Bounded Buffer Problem]] with the kernel supplying the [[Semaphores|semaphores]]:

- Buffer full and the writer keeps writing? The writer blocks into the
  [[Waiting state]] until the reader drains some.
- Buffer empty and the reader reads? The reader blocks until the writer produces.

So a pipeline self-regulates: the slowest stage sets the pace, and neither side can run
away from the other. That is [[Producer Consumer]] enforced by the operating system.

## Two kinds

- **Anonymous pipe**: created by `pipe()` and inherited across `fork()`, so it only works
  between related processes. What the shell's `|` builds.
- **Named pipe** (a [[FIFO]]): created with `mkfifo`, appears as a path in the
  [[File Systems|file system]], so any two processes can open it by name. The data still
  never hits the disk; only the name is in the file system.
